newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Afghanistan's Taleban draw shutters on photography.
newsitem.headline: Afghanistan's Taleban draw shutters on photography.

text.p: Afghanistan's purist Islamic Taleban have told news agencies and television crews that they cannot photograph or film "living bodies".
The foreign ministry sent a letter to news organisations in Kabul detailing "an order from the high authorities".
"...Photography and filming of living bodies is forbidden and is against the Sharia (the Islamic legal code) of the Islamic State of Afghanistan," it says.

Since the Taleban first appeared in Afghanistan more than two years ago, they have taken a strong line on television and photography, symbolically hanging television sets in their southern Afghan stronghold of Kandahar, and in one case smashing a television crew's equipment.
They say the depiction of living forms is forbidden under Islamic law, although photographic shops are still open in Kabul for passport photographs.
The Taleban, who now control more than three quarters of Afghanistan and captured Kabul in September, have vowed to impose strict Islamic Sharia law on the country.
A German television crew recently asked the Taleban's acting Minister of Information what they were allowed to film.
"It is permissable to film empty buildings and landscapes, as long as there are no people or animals in view," Information Minister Amir Khan Mutaqi said.

However, as is common in Taleban-held Kabul, the implementation of the order has been patchy. A French Television crew was last week granted permission to film an interview with a senior member of the Foreign Ministry.
The only aspect of the order that has been consistently implemented is the ban on photographs of women.
Soon after taking Kabul, the Taleban said it was an obligation for all Moslem men to grow a beard.
On Wednesday they said they would start to punish men who trimmed their beards.
Taleban authorities have also ordered women not to venture outside the home without their burqa, a shroud-like head-to-toe veil with a small patch of gauze over the eyes.

The militia has been battling an alliance consisting of forces loyal to the government they ousted from Kabul, the northern forces of General Abdul Rashid Dostum and Shi'ite fighters under Karim Khalili in the centre of the country.
The Taleban have yet to be recognised as the legitimate government by any country or international body.
